title: Generative AI Acceptable Use & Data Loss Prevention Pattern
description: A pattern combining a specific, example-driven acceptable-use policy for third-party generative AI tools with a technical control that actually blocks or flags disallowed data categories, rather than relying on employee compliance alone.
problem: A written policy telling employees not to paste confidential data into third-party AI tools relies entirely on individual judgement under time pressure, and provides no actual barrier when an employee pastes source code or sensitive notes into a chatbot to solve an immediate problem.
solution: Pair a specific acceptable-use policy — naming concrete disallowed data categories with examples, not abstract principles — with a technical control such as browser/endpoint data-loss-prevention tooling that flags or blocks known-sensitive patterns (source code signatures, internal document markings) before they leave the network, or provisioning an enterprise-tier tool with contractual no-training/no-retention terms as the sanctioned alternative.
applicability: Any organisation permitting employee use of third-party generative AI tools, particularly where employees routinely handle proprietary source code, trade secrets, or regulated data.
consequences: DLP tooling produces false positives that can block legitimate use and require a triage process; an approved enterprise-tier alternative has licensing cost and still requires employees to actually use it instead of a personal account.

citations.title: Samsung Bans ChatGPT, Google Bard, Other Generative AI Use by Staff After Leak

relationships.reason: A named policy owner and enforced technical control is the accountability structure this control describes.
The pattern's output is an acceptable-use policy attestation and DLP configuration record.
